USES OF THE PREMISES - The LESSEE shall not use the leased premises for dwelling or sleeping purposes. The premises hereby leased shall be used exclusively by the LESSEE for office, stockroom and related purposes and the latter shall not divert the prernises to any other uses without the prior consent of the LESSOR, it being expressly agreed that if, at any time during the existence of this Iease and without the previous consent of the LESSOR the said prernises is used for any other purposes, the LESSOR reserves the right or choice to, (a) rescind this contract in accordance with Paragraph 17, (b) increase the rental, or (c) compel the LESSEE to stop its new activities. 4. IMPROVEMENT AND ALTERATIONS - The LESSEE shall not make any alterations, installations, additions or improvements of the leased premises, suclr as partitions, shades, swings, blinds, window guards, etc., without the consent of the LESSOR. [t is further agreed 7b I \ Page2 - Contract of Lease that all such alterations, installatiorrs, additions or improvements, except movable fumiture and fixtures, placed at the expense of the LESSEE and removable without defacing or injuring tlre leased premises, shall, if so elected by the LESSOR, become its property and shall rernain, and be surrendered with the premises as part of thereof, upon termination of the lease, without compensation to the LESSEE. If the LESSOR does not elect to retain such alteration, installations, additions or improvements, the premises shall be surrendered to their original condition at the expense of the LESSEE. The LESSOR reserves the right to refuse any alteration, installation, addition or improvement requested by the LESSEE if in the LESSOR'S opinion, there is just cause to warrant such refusal. 5. POWER CONSUMPTION AND CHARGES FOR UTILITIES All electrical consumption and charges, fees and costs for telephone, water and other utilities used by the LESSEE in the leased premises, shall be for its account. The LESSEE may, at its discretion, install a separate meter and convenience outlets and all electrical connections as it may deem necessary. 6. SIGNS AND ADVERTISEMENTS - To insure uniformity of design, the LESSEE shall not cause to be affixed, inscribed or painted, any notice, sign or other advertising medium, on any part of the building without the consent of the LESSOR. The LESSEE shall not permit or give consent to any other person or entity to advertise, as if said person or entity uses, holds office, or is otherwise established, at the premises leased, or ally part thereof, and unless the LESSOR agrees to the contrary, only the name and nomenclature of the LESSEE as written in the contract of lease shall be placed in the building directory and advertised at or near the main door of the premises leased. No other sign or advertisement may be placed in the leased premises other than the place herein above indicated. 7. CARE OF THE LEASED PREMISES - The LESSEE shall maintain the leased premises in a clean and sanitary condition, free from noxious odors and disturbing noise, and upon expiration of the lease, shall surrender and return the leased premises and fixtures in as good condition, except ordinary wear and tear, as the leased premises were actually found at the beginrring of the lease. 8. The LESSEE shall indernnif, and hold harmless the said LESSOR against all actions, suits, damages and claims by whosoever they may be brought or made by reason of the nonobservance or non-performance of the said rules, regulations, ordinances, or laws, or of any covenants of this SECTION, without prejudice to the right of the LESSOR to cancelthis lease in accordance with the penal provisions hereinafter contained. 9. text: Eligible Projects Eligible projects for the PC Fund Subsidy are those that support the national priorities of the present administration aligned to the Philippine Development Plan 2011-2016 such as those achieving the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs); preparedness in disasters and adaptation to climate change; sustainable environmental management; local economic development and transparent and accountable local governance, which are implementable within one (1) year from the date of receipt of the Notice to Implement (NTI) signed by the DILG Regional Office.
title: Ordinance No. 0141-17

text: Delineation of Responsibilities PCF Recipient LGU shall: 1. Maintain a book of accounts for the PD Fund; 2. Issue an official receipt corresponding to the amount of PC fund subsidy received; 3. Crate a PCF project team responsible for the implementation of the project; 4. Submit to the DILG Regional Office thru channels the complete documentary and reportorial requirements of the proposed project/s and repofts as stipulated in memorandum Circular No. 2015 dated 5. The maximum completion of the proposed project is 12 months and must start on the date of the receipt of the Notice to Implement from the DILG Regional Offlce; 6. Put up a signage of the reports using formats such as billboards, tarpaulins, banners, or posters in the place where the project is being implemented following the template/design stipulated in COA Circular No. 2013-004. 7. For disclosure of projects, post in conspicuous places within public buildings (in front of provincial capitol, city/municipal halls, public library, market, etc.) monthly/quarterly progress of project implementation and completed projects, including the disbursed PCF subsidy. In the absence of a website (in the case of cities/municipalities), said documents shall be posted on the website of the provincial government or on the DILG regional websites. DILG Regional Office shall: 1. Prepare and issue checks as financial subsidy to the LGU beneficiary; 2. Facilitate the release of PCF check amounting to P 5,000,000.00 to the recipient LGU upon signing of this Memorandum of Agreement (MOA); 3. Issue a Notice to Implement (NTI) to the LGU recipient upon the submission of documentary requirements; 4. In coordination with the Provincial PCF Focal Person, Cluster Head, and C/MLGOO, conduct periodic monitoring on the progress of project implementation and disbursement of the PC funds by the LGU; 5. Conduct validation and ocular inspection of the LGU projects to validate reports submitted and substantiate comments/observations and recommendations. In case of negative findings and observations or slippage, the LGU beneficiary shall be required to submit an exception report that contains the negative finding and observations or slippage, its cause/s, recommendations, actions taken; 6. Post the status of project implementation and fund utilization on the DILG Regional website if needed; a { a 7. Supervise the encoding of the LGU project details, accomplishments and status at the PCF website in coordination with the Provincial PCF Focal Person, Cluster Head, and C/MLGOO as per MC No. 2015 dated This agreement shall take effect immediately upon signing by the representatives of the Parties hereto and shall be enforced within one (1) year of completion of the project. text: Roles and Responsibilities of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DswD) Pursuant to this agreement, it shall be the role and responsibility of the DSWD to; 1. text: DECLARATION OF POUCY - It is the policy of the State, under the Local Government Code (Republic Act No. 7L60), that every local government unit shall exercise the powers expressly granted, those necessarily implied therefrom, as well as powers necessary, appropriate, or incidental for its efficient and effective governance, and those which are essential to the promotion of the general welfare. Fufthermore, local government units have the power and responsibility to ensure and suppoft, among other things, the maintenance of peace and order within their respective territorial jurisdictions. Likewise, consistent with the Human Security Act (Republic Act No. 9372), it is a declared policy of the State to protect life, libefi, and property from acts of terrorism, to condemn terrorism as inimical and dangerous to the national security of the country and to the welfare of the people, and to make terrorism a crime against the Filipino people, against humanity, and against the law of nations. sEcrIoN 4. PROHIBTTED Acrs - It shall be unlawful for any person to: a) Recruit another person to membership to terrorist groups, international or local, such as but not limited to ISIS, AL-QAEDA, and MAUTE GROUp; b) Be a member of terrorist groups, international or local and actively pafticipate in any unlawful activity; c) Manufacture, possession, and distribution of any reading materials, propaganda, paraphernalia, such as flag, clothing, stickers which are related to terrorist groups, international or local; sEcrIoN 5. DEFINTTIoN oF TERMS: For purposes of this ordinance: a) ISIS refers to the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, a terrorist organization known for its human rights abuses, hate crimes, cruelty, massacre, rape, and forced religious conversions. b) AI-Qaeda means "The Base", "The Foundation" or "The Fundament,,. It refers to the militant Sunni Islamist multi-national organization founded in 19BB by Osama bin Laden, Abdullah Azzam and several other Arab volunteers who fought against the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in the 1980s. Al-Qaeda operates as network made up of Islamic extremists, Salafist jihadists. It has been designated as a terrorist group by the United Nations Security Council, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization Ord. No. 0230 -t7 (NATO), the European Union, the United States, Russia, India, various other countries. Al-Qaeda has mounted attacks on civilian military targets in various countries. d) TERRORIST GROUP - refers to any organization, association or group of persons or any entity owned or controlled by any terrorist or group that: (1) commits, or attempts to commit, terrorist acts by any means, directly or indirectly, unlawfully or willfully; (2) pafticipates as an accomplice in terrorist acts; (3) organizes or directs others to commit terrorist acts; (4) contributes to the commission of terrorist acts by a group of persons acting with common purpose of fufthering the terrorist acts where the contribution is made intentionally and with the aim of fufthering the terrorist acts or with the knowledge of the intention of the group to commit terrorist acts.

text: GENERAL PROVISTONS. a. Appraisal by Stripping Method shall be adopted where 100o/o base value per square meter on residential and commercial lands shall be applied within the first strip fronting roads or streets. Land beyond the standard depth, that is, 20m for residential, 30m for commercial and 50m for industrial shall be valued at 80o/o for the 2nd strip, 600/o for the 3d strip, 40o/o for the 4h strip, 20o/o for the 5h strip of the base value fixed for the road or street thereof for the remaining area, provided that, the value per square meter of the last strip shall not be lower than the value per square meter of lots in the other street or of the interior lots as reflected in the Schedule of Market Value. Stripping Method shall not apply to corner lots if the sides are less than the standard depth. b, Subdivision lots are not subject to stripping. c. For abnormally low lands, a reduction from the base unit value may be allowed in the amount to the cost of fllling-up of such land, provided that, such deduction shall not exceed 30o/o of the value of the lot subject to appraisal if it were normally filled or leveled. d. Corner influence of 100/o of the base unit value shall be added to residential and commercial lots situated at the corner of the streets or roads. Provided that, if the streets or roads have different base unlt value, the higher value shall be used in the computation. An alley or callejon shall not be considered for the adjustment thereof. e. Roads or streets in urban subdivisions, unless already donated or turned over to the barangay or city, shall be listed in the name of the subdivision owner and shall be valued on the basis of the actual condition and cost of cementing, asphalting or paving them with gravel and sand per square meter. f. Vacant lands shall be classified, valued and assessed like similar lands in the area. g. Urban land fully occupied by squatters who prevented the owner from using or making developments of the subject lot, park and open spaces shall be valued at 50o/o of the base value. Ord. No. 0257-17 h. Interior lots shall be valued at 50% of the base value of the lots fronting primary road or street, however stripping method shall not be applied. i. Triangular lot with its base on the street shall be computed as a regular lot with 70olo base value. j. Triangular lot with its apex on the street shall be computed as a regular lot with 30% base value. k. Trapezoid Lots shall be computed based on the values of the rectangular and triangular portions separately and to take the sum of the computed values for the total value. m. Lots along concrete roads shall have a 100o/o base value,95% base value for dirt road and 80% base value for alley and proposed road. 2. Appraisal of Agricultural Lands (a)The unit base value per hectare prescribed in the SMV is multiplied by the area of the agricultural land to arrive at the market value for the different kinds and sub-classes of agricultural lands. Apparently, the kind of plants and trees determine the classification and value of the agricultural land. The aggregate value arrived at is subject to applicable adjustments expressed in percentage, to wit: (1) Type of Road % Adjustment (a) Provincial or national road (b) For all-weather roads No deduction 3% deduction c Alo dirt roads 6% deduction d For no road outlet 9% deduction (2) Location Distance in Km to: (a) All weather roads (b) Local Trading Center (Poblacion) 0to 1 +SYo Over 1 to 3 -2% 0% Over 3 to 6 -2Yo -6% -4Yo Over 9 -8% -6% l. Irregular Lot shall be computed by reducing the irregular lot to the nearest equivalent rectangular, triangular and trapezoidal sections and apply the foregoing rules in computing lot values, -4% Over 6 to 9 Ord. No. 0257-17 The distance of a property from all-weather roads, landing places along sea coasts and from a trading center or poblacion shall be measured from the corner of the lot or parcel nearest to such road or center. All weather roads include national, provincial, municipal and all other public roads traversable by trucks, cars and other forms of vehicles under any kind of weather. (b)The computation of values begins with the determination of the area, productivity and sub-class or sub-classes of an agricultural land. In the case of a parcel of land utilized or planted to various agricultural crops, such as, rice, corn, coconut, etc. (if practicable, the boundaries between each sub-class shall be plotted or sketched on the map) and the corresponding area thereof be determined. Each area so determined shall be multiplied by the applicable unit base value. The resulting values for each sub-class so computed are summed up to obtain the total base market value of the parcel. To arrive at a final value, the total base market value is multiplied by the adjustment percentage, as stated above. (c) Values of improvement such as plants and trees shall be considered in the preparation of the Schedule of Values for agricultural lands. Although these crops are deemed improvemenG to the land, they shall not be appraised apart from the land as they are an integral part thereof and their value is inherent or forms part of the land. However, if it shall be proven that the ownership of the land is different from that of the improvement, a separate valuation and assessment shall be made in the names of the respective owners. (d)Agricultural land convertible into residential subdivisions, commercial or industrial land shall be classified and valued as agricultural until such time that they shall have been actually converted and developed into such. This rule shall also apply to lands already approved by proper authorities as subdivisions but have not yet been actually developed for the purpose. As soon as a portion of the subdivision is finally divided, converted and developed into residential lots, the same shall be valued like similar lots in the locality. Portions of the subdivisions not yet developed and converted into residential, commercial or industrial lot shall remain to be classified and valued as agricultural. Portions of agricultural land not yet developed, converted and actually used as residential, commercial or industrial shall remain to be classified and valued as agricultural. 3. Appraisal of Timber and Forest Lands llmber and forest lands belonging to the Republic of the Philippines or any of its political subdivisions, the beneficial use of which have been granted to a taxable person, shall be subject to the real property tax. For this purpose, said lands shall be appraised and assessed yearly against the beneficial useratthe market value ofthe marketable timber on the Ord. No. 0257-77 basis of the annual volume of timber "actually cut" from the operational area, during the preceding year, regardless of the annual total .'allowable cut" indicated in the lease agreement. 4. Appraisal of Mineral Lands (a) Mineral lands are those lands in which minerals exist in sufficient quantity or grade to justify the necessary expenditures to be incurred in extracting and utilizing such minerals. (b) Mineral lands are further classified as follows: 2. Non-Metallic Mineral Lands These are lands which contain all other deposits not covered by the above-deflned metallic elements or minerals. (c) Mineral Lands shall be appraised yearly against the beneficial user or concessionaire on the basis of the value of extracted minerals. 5. Appraisal of Buildings (a) For the appraisal of buildings and other structures, the schedule of Base Unit construction cost (SBUCC) shall be used. The sBUCC refers to the base unit construction cost of buildings per square meter including the additional/deduction items as may be determined by the assessor. However, buildings and other structures not included in the sBucc shall be appraised based on the actual cost (b) In case of a multi-storey building used both for residential and commercial or industrial purposes, the same shall be classified and valued in accordance with the type of building provided in the schedule of Base unit construction Cost and shall be assessed on the basis of the actual use of such building. (c) Bowling alleys shall be initially valued separately from the principal building but its appraisal/assessment shall finally form part of the whole building, except the machinery, which shall be covered by a separate appraisal and assessment. (d) In case of buildings and structures already covered by existing assessment, the Reproduction/Replacement Cost New Less Depreciation (RCNLD) approach shall be applied. (e) Inspection Levels - The level of property inspection depends on the quality of the Field Appraisal Assessment Sheet (FAAS's) and various other factors such as: 1. Metallic Mineral Lands These are lands which contain any of the metallic elements or minerals, or their combinations such as gold, silver, platinum, tin, chromium, iron, manganese, copper, nickel, lead, zinc, tungsten, and the like. Ord. No. 0257-t7 1, Years of last re-appraisal/revision of assessment; 2. Level of new construction; 3. Local changes; 4. Higher than normal appeal activity; 5. Inconsistent or incorrect classification of buildings or land; 6. Changes in the market area such as area redevelopment, increased density, use or zoning; 7. The need to redefine market area boundaries and establish new benchmarks; 8. Change in market preferences for factors such as house style/age, lot size, market area characteristics, traffic patterns, etc; 9. Changes in building costs because of changes in code requirements, new materials/designs, etc; and 10, Changes in market perception from positive or negative factors; Correcting appraisal deficiencies generally require some level of physical inspection of the property. Different levels of inspection will be required depending upon the reason(s) found for the deficiency. The following are generally accepted definitions for the various levels of inspections: Level 1. A full inspection is made with a full interior inspection. Level 2. An exterior inspection is made. No attempt at an interior inspection is made unless a major change to the property is detected. Level 3. A street inspection is conducted. (Drive-by inspection only, unless a major change to the property is detected.) 6. Appraisal of Machinery and Equipment (a) The appraisal of machinery for tax purposes shall be based on its actual cost to the owner. To support the actual cost, the declared value or sworn statement from the owner or responsible officer, in case of a corporation, shall be secured to form as an integral part of the appraisal report. (b) For imported brand new machinery, the market value shall be based on its acquisition cost, which is the actual cost to the owner when the same is not yet depreciated or appraised within the year of its purchase, plus the costs of freigh,t, insurance, bank and other charges, brokerage, arrastre and handling, duties and taxes, plus the costs of inland transpoftation, handling and installation charges at the present site. The cost in foreign currency shall be converted to peso cost on the basis of the foreign currency exchange rates when such machinery was actually purchased as fixed by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). Level 4. No on-site inspection is made. Ord. No. 0257-17 (c) By the expressed provision of the Local Government Code, the acquisition cost of the machinery shall be based on the actual cost to the owner when it was acquired. The cost in foreign currency shall be converted to peso cost based on the foreign exchange rate then prevailing when the same was acquired. (d) In all other cases, the cost in foreign currency of imported machinery shall be converted to peso equivalent based on exchange rates flxed by the BSp at the time of acquisition and apply a depreciation allowance of not exceeding five percent (5%) per year. (0 Depreciation allowance for machinery shall be made at a rate not exceeding five percent (50/o) of its original cost or its replacement or reproduction cost, as the case may be, for each year of use: Provided, however, that the remaining value for all kinds of machinery shall be fixed at not less than twenty percent (20o/o) of such original, replacement, or reproduction cost for so long as the machinery is useful and operational. (g) Transmission Lines, Transmission Towers, Cell Sites and the like shall be assessed like all other machineries and taxes thereon shall be paid to the local government unit where they are constructed. Transmission lines including the posts shall be appraised on the basis of its total value using the cost or income approach and the total market value shall also be apportioned or pro-rated between the local government units where these lines traverse. (h) Submerged pipe lines for natural gas, water, etc., shall be appraised on the basis of the cost or income approach, the total market value thereof shall be apportioned or pro-rated between the local government units they traverse. Ord. No. 0257-17 (i) Reservoirs, dams, tailing ponds, piers and wharyes shall be appraised on the basis of the cost approach, Provided, however, that the cost of pilings on ports must be given additional consideration. 7. Appraisal of Special Purpose Properties (1) Special purpose properties such as golf course, memorial park, cemeteries, hospitals, schools, malls, shopping centers, gasoline stations and condominiums, are properties which are designed, constructed and developed for a specific use or purpose. By its very nature the type of property is rarely offered for sale in the open market as part of a going concern. Due to its special design and function, conversion of special purpose properties to other types of development or application is generally not economically feasible. (2) In valuing special purpose properties, the appraiser shall be guided with the provisions in SECTION 8, Chapter IV of the Local Assessment Regulation (LAR) 1-04 issued by the Bureau of Local Government Finance - Department of Finance (BLGF-DOF). C. Rules in the Assessment of Real Property All real propertles, whether taxable or exempt, shall be appraised based on the applicable Schedule of Market Values for Lands (SMV) and Base Unit Construction Cost (BUCC) prepared by the City Assessor. Real property declared for the first time shall be assessed for the period during which it would have been liable but in no case for more than ten (10) years prior to the date of initial assessment: Provided, however, that such taxes shall be computed on the basis of the applicable schedule of values in force during the corresponding period. Provided further, that the total tax liability shall include the current year in addition to the ten (10) years back taxes. If such taxes are paid on or before the end of the quarter following the date the notice of assessment was received by the owner or his representative, no interest for delinquency shall be imposed thereon; otheruvise, such taxes shall be subject to an interest at the rate of two percent (2o/o) per month or a fraction thereof until such taxes are fully paid. 1. Assessment of Lands (a) Lands actually and principally used for residential, agricultural, commercial, industrial or mineral purposes, shall be classified and valued according to the schedule of unit base market values and assessed at their corresponding levels of assessment. (b) Lands located in areas of mixed land uses such as residential with commercial or industrial, the predominant use of the lands in that area shall govern the classification and valuation thereof. If the predominant use is residential, all lands in that area shall be classified as residential; if the predominant use is commercial or industrial, all lands in that area shall be classified as such. Ord. No. 0257-77 (c) A lot or parcel of land classified and appraised as commercial or industrial occupied by a building used both for residential and commercial or industrial purposes shall be assessed on the basis of the predominant use of the building or buildings. If the predominant use of the building is residential, the assessment level fixed thereon for residential land shall be applied on the market value of the lot or parcel determined on the basis ofthe schedule of base market values; if industrial or commercial, the assessment level for industrial or commercial shall be applied on the basis of the schedule of base market values. (d) Vacant lands shall be assessed like similar lands in the locality. (e) Lands owned by local water districts and government-owned or controlled corporations rendering essential public services in the supply and distribution of water and/or generation and transmission of electric power, located in residential, commercial or industrial area shall be assessed as special property at ten percent (100/o) assessment level applied to the market value. If those special classes of lands are, however, located in areas of mixed land uses, such as residential with commercial or industrial, the predominant use of the lands in that area of those special classes of land shall be assessed at the corresponding levels of assessment. (f) Lands actually, directly and exclusively used for religious, charitable or educational purposes located in residential, commercial or industrial areas shall be assessed as residential, commercial or industrial, as the case may be. If those lands actually, directly and exclusively used for religious, charitable or educational purposes are, however, located in an area of mixed land uses, such as residential with commercial or industrial, the predominant use of the lands in that area shall govern the classification of those lands used for religious, charitable or educational purposes. However, if those lands are occupied by a building used both for educational, residential, commercial or Industrial, the area of land occupied by the building and its premises shall be assessed as residential, commercial or industrial as the case may be. (g) Reclassification of Lands to Other Uses 1. Land converted into other uses, e,g. agricultural to residential, residential to commercial, made known to the assessor in writing by the owner shall be inspected for confirmation of the actual condition/use of the property; Ord. No. 0257-t7 2. A report of the actual condition of the property and the recommendation thereof shall be rendered by the responsible personnel. Such report shall be submitted within ten (10) working days after inspection in accordance with the policy as may be prescribed by the City Assessor; 3. Among others, the report may contain information regarding tangible land improvement, e.g. land leveling and compaction, construction of road networks, drainage and other relevant land amenities; 4. In all other cases, Local Finance Circular No. 3-92 dated September LL, 1992 shall be controlling in reclassifying agricultural lands to non-agricultural uses; and 5. A duly approved Zoning Ordinance also serves as basis in the reclassifi cation of lands. 6. Sworn statement declaring the true value and classiflcation by the owner. 2. Assessment of Buildings and Other tmprovements (a) Buildings used exclusively for residential purposes shall be classified and valued in accordance with the schedule of base unit construction cost, and shall be assessed by applying the corresponding assessment levels fixed by ordinances of the SANGGUNIANG panlungsod. (b)A one-storey building used both for residential and commercial or industrial purposes shall be classified and valued in accordance with the schedule of base unit construction cost and shall be assessed on the basis of the predominant use of the building. (c) A multi-storey building used both for residential and commercial or industrial and any other purposes shall be classified and valued in accordance with the type of building provided in the SBUCC and shall be assessed on the basis of its actual use. (d) Buildings and other improvements actually, directly and exclusively used for hospitals, cultural or scientific purposes shall be classified and valued according to the schedule of base unit construction cost, and shall be assessed at 15olo of their depreciated market values. (e) Buildings owned by local water districts and Government-Owned or Controlled Corporations rendering essential public services in the supply and distribution of water and/or generation and transmission of electric power shall, likewise be classified and valued in accordance with the schedule of base unit construction cost, and shall be assessed at 10o/o of their depreciated value. Ord. No. 0257-17 (f,) Churches, parsonages, convents, mosques and buildings and other improvements used actually, directly and exclusively for religious, charitable or educational purposes shall be classified and valued in accordance with the schedule of base unit construction cost, if applicable, othenrrise on the basis of their replacement cost as of the year of appraisal, and shall be assessed as residential on the basis of their depreciated values. (g) Buildings and other improvements owned by the Republic of the Philippines or any of its political subdivisions shall be classified, valued and assessed like similar buildings and improvements in the locality. If the buildings and improvements are of a kind not covered by the schedule of base unit construction cost, they shall be valued at their fair market value at the time of appraisal and shall be assessed like similar buildings and improvements in the locality. D. Notice of New or Revised Assessments (1) When real propefi is assessed for the first time or when an existing assessment is increased or decreased, the City Assessor shall within thirty (30) days give written notice of such new or revised assessment to the person in whose name the property is declared. (2)Although the real property tax is levied against real property, it is the owner who pays the tax. Before the tax liability is fixed, the property owner is entitled to a hearing on the assessment of the property; notice and hearing constitute part of the due process (not strictly judicial) in taxation. If the owner is not satisfied with the action of the assessor in the assessment of the property, the said owner can resoft to the appeals process provided in Chapter VII of Local Assessment Regulation (LAR) 1-04. If he does not appeal within the said period, he will be deprived of his right to be heard by the Board of Assessment Appeals (LBAA). However, in cases where a request is made by the person in whose name the propefty is declared to correct erroneous or illegal assessments, the Assessor, after re-inspection and report of actual condition and recommendation by responsible personnel, may correct and adjust the assessment previously made without necessarily referring to LBAA. But, once the Notice of Re-Assessment has been sent to the propefty owner, assessment/re-assessment is beyond the authority of the assessor and is already under the jurisdiction of the Local Board of Assessment Appeals (LBAA). a. The written notice together with the owner's copy of the tax declaration shall be addressed to the person in whose name the propefty is declared. It may be delivered personally or to the occupant in possession of the property, or by mail to the last known address of the owner or thru the assistance of the punong barangay. Ord. No. 0257-17 b. If personally delivered to the owner or person in possession of the property, the person serving the notice shall secure the signature of the owner or occupant on the duplicate copy of the notice, with a notation of the date when the notice was served and whether recipient is the owner or occupant of the property. If assistance of the punong barangay is secured, the signature should appear on the duplicate copy of the notice. The duplicate copies of the notice of assessments signed by the owners or occupants of the property and the registry return cards shall be flled in the office of the city assessor and annotated on the Field Appraisal Assessment Sheet (FAAS) that such Notice of Assessment (NOA) has been issued indicating the name of the person who received the Notice of Assessment (NOA), date and time received, These are important in asceftaining whether appeals filed by owners of real property are filed within the reglamentary period of sixty days from the date of receipt of such notices.

Article 2 Scope of Cooperation The parties shall undertake to implement this MoU in accordance with the laws and regulation of their respective countries in the environmental fields as follows: a. Low Carbon Society; b. Resource recycling, c. Capacity Building for the officials of each city; d. Other fields of cooperation as mutually agreed upon by the Parties in writing Article 3 Tech n ica I Arra ngements To facilitate the implementation of this MoU, the Parties may conclude arangements within the terms of this tt/oU, which shall cover the fields as provided in Article 2 ; 2. Such arrangements shall be in conformity with this lVoU, and shall describe program or project schedule, personnel involved, financial arrangements, responsibilities undertaken by the Parties and other necessary details; 3. The Parties may invite the third party to take parl in implementation of the field as stated in article 2 as well as arrangement of the involvement of the third party in each program to create the mutually beneficial cooperation in both cities Article 4 Fina ncial Arrangements The implementation of the actrvities under this MoU is subject to the availability of fund and personnel of the Parties. 2. Unless otherwise agreed by the Parties, each Party shall bear its cost to implement this MoU. Article 5 Joint Working GrouP 1. The Parties may establish a Joint Working Group to plan, prepare and recommend program as well as monitor and evaluate the progress of cooperation under this MoU; 2, The members of the Joint Working Group shall consist of representatives of the respective governments The Joint Working Group may invite the private sector to take part in its deliberation, if necessary and subject to mutual consent of the Parties; 3. The Joint Working Group shall meet in Davao or in Kitakyushu as necessary Article 6 lntellectual PropertY Rights 1. Each Party shall protect intellectual property rights of other Party in accordance with the relevant domestic laws and regulations in force in their respective country; 2. ln case of specific arrangements, program or project result in the intellectual property, such property shall be jointly owned, and the Parties shall conclude separate arrangement to govern such property in accordance with the laws and regulations of the respective countries; 3. lf either Party wishes to disclose confidential data and or information furnished by the other party or created by the Parties in the implementation of this MoU, the disclosing Party shall obtained written consent from the other Party prior to the disclosure of such data and or information. Article 7 Limitation of Personnel Activities The Pa'rties shall ensure that their personnel engaged in activities under this MoU shall respect and comply with the laws and regulations of the host party's country, shall have the obligation not to interfere the domestic affairs of the country of the host party and shall refrain from conducting activities inconsistent with the objective of this MoU. Article B Suspension Each Party reserves the right, for reasons of national security, national interest, public order or public health, to suspend temporarily, either in whole or in a part, the implementation of this MoU. The suspension shall take effect immediately after notification has been given to the other Party. Article 9 Settlement of Disputes Any differences arising out of the interpretation or implementation of this lVoU shall be settled amicably through consultation and/or negotiation between the Parlies. text: DEFINITION OF TERMS. - For the purpose of this Ordinance, the following terms and phrases shall apply: 2.L. Protection Order - refers to an order issued under the Act for the purpose of preventing further acts of violence against a woman or her child specifled in SECTION 7 of the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) and granting other necessary relief. Barangay Protection Order (BPO)- refers to the protection order issued by the Punong Barangay (PB) or if the PB is unavailable, by a kagawad ordering the offender to desist from committing or threatening physical harm to the victim. It is effective for 15 days and is not extendible. a Permanent Protection Order (PPO) - refers to the protection order issued by the court after notice and hearing. Temporary Protection Order (TPO) - refers to the protection order issued by the court on the date of filing of the application after ex parte determination that such order should be issued. A couft may grant in a TPO any, some or all of the reliefs mentioned in the Act and shall be effective for thirty (30) days. The court shall schedule a hearing on the issuance of a PPO prior to or on the date of the expiration of the TPO. The court shall order the immediate personal seruice of the TPO on the respondent by the couft sheriff who may obtain the assistance of law enforcement agents for the service. The TPO shall include notice of the date of the hearing on the merits of the issuance of a PPO; 2.2. Violence Against Women (VAW) - refers to any act of gender-based violence that results in, or is likely to result in physical, sexual, or psychological harm or suffering to women, including threats of such acts, coercion, or arbitrary deprivation of liberty, whether occurring in public or in private life. It shall be understood to encompass, but not limited to, the following: Physical, sexual, psychological, and economic violence occurring in the family, including battering, sexual abuse of female children in the household, dowryrelated violence, marital rape, and other traditional practices harmful to women, non-spousal violence and violence related to exploitation; Physical, sexual and psychological violence occurring within the general community, including rape, sexual abuse, sexual harassment, and intimidation at work, in educational institutions and elsewhere, trafficking in women, and prostitution; and physical, sexual, and psychological violence perpetrated or condoned by the State, wherever it occurs. It also includes acts of violence against women as defined in Republic Act Nos. 9208 and 9262. Under the Magna Cafta of Women, this term is used interchangeably with gender-based violence; 2.3. VAW Desk - a facility that would address VAW cases in a genderresponsive manner, managed by a person designated by the punong barangay. It is situated within the premises of the barangay hall. In the absence of a barangay hall, the VAW Desk shall be established within the premises where the punong barangay holds office; The definition of terms provided in Republic Act No. 9710, otherwise known as the Magna Carta of Women, as far as applicable, are hereby made part of this Ordinance. a I Ord. No. 0310-17
title: Ordinance No. 0310-17

text: SCOPE AND COVERAGE. - This Ordinance shall be enforced within all barangays of the City of Davao;
title: Ordinance No. 0310-17

text: ESTABLISHMENT OF VAW DESK IN EVERY BARANGAY. 4.1. Setting up the VAW Desk - the punong barangay shall designate an area within the barangay hall for VAW desk. She/He shall provide for the necessary furniture and fixtures such as, but not limited to, table, chairs, separate filing cabinet and log books for record-keeping of cases. Likewise, the punong barangay shall ensure the confidentiality of the case and privacy and safety of the victim-survivor. 4.2. Designation of vAW Desk person the punong barangay shall designate a VAW desk person who is trained in gender-sensitive handling of cases; preferably a woman barangay kagawad or a woman barangay tanod. In cases where there are no trained personnel, ensure that the person assigned shall undergo basic gender-sensitivity training and orientation on anti-VAW laws;
title: Ordinance No. 0310-17

text: FUNCTIONS OF THE BARANGAY VAW DESK. Given the many functions of the Barangay VAW Desk (BVD), the VAW Desk Officer must report for duty from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. to respond to complaints and assist clients. The VAW Desk Officer must be accessible through landline and mobile phones and should be on call in case an accident occurs after working hours. The VAW Desk shall perform the following tasks: 5.1. Respond to gender-based violence cases brought to the barangay; 5.2. Keep VAW case records confidential and secured, and ensure that only authorized personnel can access it; 5.3. Assist victims of VAW in securing Barangay Protection Order (BPO) and in accessing necessary seruices; 5.4. Develop the barangay's gender-responsive plan in addressing gender-based violence, including support services, capacity building and referral system; 5.5. Coordinate with and refer cases to government agencies, nongovernment organizations (NGOs), institutions, and other seruice providers as necessary; 5.5. Address other forms of abuse committed against women, especially senior citizens, women with disabilities, and other marginalized groups; 5.7. Lead advocacies on the elimination of VAW in the community; and 5.8. Perform other related functions as may be assigned;
title: Ordinance No. 0310-17

text: PROTOCOL IN HANDLING VAW CASES AT THE BARANGAY LEVEL. The following protocols shall be observed by the Barangay VAW Desk person when responding to VAW situations: 6.1. A victim-survivor is accompanied by someone to the barangay or personally goes to the barangay: 6.1.1. Make the woman (and child/children, if applicable) comfortable in a safe and private room, giving her water and other immediate needs, if any; 6.1.2. Assess the situation and get initial information to determine the risks on hand and if immediate medical attention is needed. If so, facilitate referral to the nearest medical facility; Ord. No. 0310-17 6.1.3. After the victim-survivor has stabilized, assist the punong barangay/kagawad in the conduct of an investigation in a gender-sensitive and nonjudgmental manner in a language understood by her; 6.1.4. Inform her of her rights, the remedies available and the processes involved particularly in relation to the Barangay protection order (BpO). Assist her to file an application, if she so decides to obtain a BpO; 6.1.5. Record the incident using the Barangay Intake SheeU 6.1.6. If the victim-survivor desires to be in a safe shelter, seek the assistance of other barangay officials, barangay tanod or the police in getting her belongings and refer her to a shelter/women's center or to the City Social Seruices and Development Office (CSSDO); 6,1.7. Assist the victim-surivor to file for a Temporary protection order (TPo) or Permanent Protection order (PPo) with the nearest Famiry Court within twenty-four Qfl hours after issuance of Bpo, if the victimsurvivor so desires, or she applies directly for a TPo/PPo instead of a BPO; 6.1.8. Repoft the incident within four (4) hours to the Philippine National Police (PNP) and the city social Seruices and Development office (cssDo); 6.2. A victim-survivor of VAWC is reported by a community member: 6.2.1. Verify the information and if needed, seek assistance from the PNP; 6.2.2. Assess the situation and facilitate the rescue of the victim-sulivor when necessary to ensure her safety, and when applicable, the safety of her children; 6.2.3,Inform the victim-survivor about her rights and remedies available pafticularly with regard to the BPo and its processes. Assists her to apply for a BPO, if she so desires; 6.2.4. Refer the victim-suwivor for medical care and temporary shelter and other needs when needed, based on the assessment done; 6.2.5. Record the incident using the Barangay Intake Sheet; 6.2.6.If not done earlier, report the incident within four hours to the PNP and the CSSDO; 6.3. For rape, trafficking in persons and other cases which do not fall under the jurisdiction of the barangay, assist the victim-survivor to file a complaint at the PNP Women and Children Protection Center or the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI);

text: PARAMOUNT WARRI9R - Also called "Bawwangin" by the local tribes), Datu Bago was of Kagan, Tausug and Maguindanawon ancestry who setUed in Bagobo land (now known as Davao). He fought long and hard in keeping Davao Gulf free from foreign control as the whole area around the Gulf of Davao was under his control. In 1839, Datu Bago joined by the Bagobo and Kagan Tribes, struck his greatest blow against foreign invaders. Davao was the last unoccupied territory in the Philippines and Datu Bago heroically defended it against the Spaniards.

text: DEC1ARATION OF POUCY- The provisions of this Ordinance, in consonance with the City Governmenfs commitment for good governance and maintaining public order and safety, hereby declares this policy to strengthen the implementation of security measures imposed by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), the Philippine National Police (PNP), Rehabilitation Centers and other Law Enforcement Agencies. For this purpose, the City of Davao adheres to the following measures: a) To prevent the occurrence of deaths, riots, hostage taking and escape of inmates or patients by prohibiting the possession and entry of deadly and bladed weapons; b) To prevent the inmates or patients from coercing, intimidating, threatening complainants and witnesses or other forms of retaliation, orchestrate crimes and organize rescue plan by prohibiting the possession and entry of cellular phones and other electronic gadgets; c) To prevent the inmates or patients from bribing jail or detention center personnel or custodians by prohibiting the possession of excessive amount of money in cash or check inside jails or detention centers; d) To safeguard public health and well-being of the inmates or patients by penalizing the possession and entry of illegal drugs, alcoholic substances, cigarettes and tobaccos; and e) To promote public welfare in the community by ensuring the rehabilitation and development of inmates or patients in preparation for their eventual reintegration into the society upon release.

WITNESSETH: WHEREAS, CG-Davao has identified infrastructure development and agriculture as among the Top L0 Priority Programs of the government; WHEREAS, CG-Davao aims to rehabilitate Agdao Public Market,located at Brgy. Agdao Proper, Davao City, to provide better facilities and services to the public; WHEREAS, CG-Davao sought the assistance of the Department of Agriculture for funding of the above- mentioned proj ect; WHEREAS, Department of Agriculture through DA RFO Xt ini,tialty appropriated Two Hundred Million Pesos Only (Php 200,000,000.00) for the Construction of Agdao Farmer's Market [1st Phase), funded under its Locally Funded Project as per approved General Appropriations Act [GAA) FY 201.8, RA# 10964, the budget in the amount of Six Hundred Million Pesos [Php 600,000,000.00) for the Phase II of the project has already been provided in the National Expenditures Program for submission to Congress of the Philippines to be included in the 2019 budget of the Department of Agriculture, while the Phase III in the amount of Three Hundred Fifty Million [Php 350,000,000) for the proposed parking building will be submitted by the Department of Agriculture for corresponding budget allocation by the Department of Budget and Managemen! WHEREAS, DA RFO XI has sought the assistance of DPWH RO XI in the review of plans and quantity estimates prepared by City Engineering Office, Davao City and prepare the cost estimates including the procurement and implementation of the Project; WHEREAS, the DPWH RO XI will review the Project Plans and quantity estimates and prepare the Program of Work and Detailed Cost Estimates amounting to Two Hundred Million Pesos Only (PhP 200,000,000.00) as the Proiect Cost; WHEREAS, DPWH RO XI is willing to provide the personnel and expertise necessary for the completion of the project; NOW THEREFORE, for and in consideration of the foregoing premises, the parties hereto agree as follows: A. RESPONSIBILITIES OF CG.DAVAO L. Prepare the Detailed Cost Estimates and Quantity Estimates; yv> .1 ,2. In coordination with DA RFO XI, evaluate the recommendations made by the DPWH RO XI officials for possible changes and improvement relative to any aspect in the plans and specifications; 3. Assign personnel to monitor and supervise the implementation of the Project; 4. Coordinate with DA RFO XI and DPWH R0 XI to ensure the efficient implementation of the Project; 5. Accept the completed project upon full determination that work has been implemented in accordance with the approved plans and specifications; and 6. Manage the operations of the Agdao Farmer's Market upon completion of the Project. B. RESPONSIBILITIES OF DA RFO XI 1. Secure the necessary funding for the Construction/Rehabilitation of the Agdao Farmer's Market; 2. Execute Memorandum of Agreement between DPWH RO XI on the terms and conditions for the release of the Project Cost amounting to Two Hundred Million Pesos Only [Php 200,000,000.00) in tranches; 3. Disburse the amount equivalent to 0.5% of the contract amount intended for the administrative cost in favor of the DPWH R0 XI upon issuance of Notice of Award to the winning bidder; 4. Assign technical personnel to monitor and coordinate with CG-Davao and DPWH RO XI personnel, to supervise the implementation of the project and to conduct the necessary inspection to ensure conformity to approved plans and specifications; 5. Prepare and submit monthly status reports on the project and such other reports as may be required by the Commission on Audit [COA); 6. Issue the usual Certificate ofAcceptance and Turn-over; and 7. Turn-over to the CG-Davao the completed project. C. RESPONSIBILITIES OF DPWH RO XI 1. Review of plans and quantity estimates prepared by City Engineering Office, Davao City and prepare the cost estimates including the procurement and implementation of the Project; 2. Inform the winning bidder/contractor that the project will be supervised by DPWH R0 XI, and monitored by DA RFO XI and CG-Davao; 3. lnitiate, coordinate and supervise all activities with respect to the implementation of the project to ensure conformity with the plans and specifications and other provisions stipulated in the contract; 4. Consult with, advise, assist and recommend to DA RFO XI and CG-Davao all changes relative to any respect in the plans and speciflcations. Changes should be made after prior coordination and upon the approval of DA RFO XI and CG-Davao; 5. Conduct meetings with DA RFO XI officials and CG-Davao whenever necessary to discuss the progress of work and to promptly address problems affecting the implementation of the project; 6. Conduct jointly with rhe DA RFO XI officials and CG-Davao the final inspection of the Project for the issuance of a Certificate of Completion, and recommend acceptance of the project; 7. Submit to DA RFO XI the audited liquidation report and utilization report certified by the Accountant every time Billing Statement is given by the Contractor and return andf or reimburse the same, any and all amount not spent or used in the Project; and B. Turn-over to DA RF0 XI the completed project in accordance with the plans and specifications. D. ON ALL CONTRACTING PARTIES The CG-Davao, DA RFO XI and DPWH R0 XI agree that meetings may be called by either party anytime during the project implementation to address problems and concerns that may cause delays in the project, and to provide remedial measures and solutions thereto. E. DURATION OF THE AGREEMENT This Agreement shall be effective and binding upon the herein parties upon the execution hereol and to continue in full force and effect until completion of the Project. text: DECLARATION OF POLICY - The City Government of Davao hereby declares the following as its policies: 1. The Local Government shall protect and advance the right of all Dabawenyos to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature; 2. The Local Government shall promote conservation of our forest lands in pursuing sustainable urban development, as a crucial component to the aspirations of a livable city not only for the Dabawenyos but also for the generations to come; 3. Enhancement and protection of forest lands must be established and maintained through a pafticipative, empowered and environmentally conscious community; 4. The Local Government recognizes the important role of the community in the protection and conservation of natural resources, as well as in promoting and instilling the awareness on forest conservation and protection; 5. The Local Government recognizes the need to a balance economic growth with the protection of forest lands for the attainment of sustainable growth; and 6. The Local Government recognizes the need for a legislation to ensure the protection of our forest lands by adopting the Forest Land Use Plan as part of the Land Use plan of oavao city.

WITNESSETH: VUHEREAS, the ECCD Council is duly mandated in accordance with Republic Act L0410 (Early Years Act) to institutionalize a National System for Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) that is comprehensive, integrative and sustainable that will involve multi-sectoral and interagency collaboration at the national and local levels among government, among seruice providers, families and communities, and among the public and private sectors, non-government organizations, professional organizations and academic institutions; WHEREAS, as provided in the Early Years Act, the ECCD Council is mandated to establish National Child Development Center (NCDC's) and convert selected existing Day Care Centers into Child Development Centers (CDC); WHEREAS, the NCDC is a resource facility that shall serue as laboratory of the different modes of delivery of center-based and/or home-based ECCD programs that refer to the full range of health, nutrition, early education and social seruices developnnent programs that provide for the basic holistic needs of young children from age zero (0) to four (4) years; and to promote their optimum growth and development. WHEREAS, in pursuance of the above mandate, the ECCD Council aims to further enhance the provision of quality home-based and center-based ECCD programs by establishing National Child Development Centers in partnership with local government units (LGUs); ( WHEREAS, such partnership with LGUs shall consist of an arrangement for the conduct of ECCD programs as above defined and the construction of a fully-furnished and fullyequipped NCDC; WHEREAS, the NCDC shall be constructed and provided by the ECCDC with contents such as furniture, fixtures and other accessories, manipulative learning materials, story Lrooks and posters, musical instruments, afts and crafts, hygiene, toilet and bath and equipment; WHEREAS, as a stakeholder, the LGU shall support the establishment and operations of a NCDC in its jurisdiction through the implementation of ECCD programs in accordance with the guidelines for the operation of NCDCs that shall be promulgated by the ECCDC; V\THEREAS, in accordance with the principles of local autonomy and integrated clevelopment, there is a need to coordinate national government policies and programs with those of local government units; WHEREAS, the parties have agreed to undertake a cooperative endeavour for the establishment of a NCDC within the LGU; NOW, THEREFORE, the PARTIES agree on the following terms and conditions: ARTICLE 1 GENERAL PRINCIPLES, SCOPE AND COVERAGE 1.1 r.2 1.3 r.4 1.5 The term "Main Project" refers to the construction of NCDC to be located in Barangay (to lre idLntified yet) within the Davao City with an estimated proieci cost of TWO MILLION THREE HUNDRED THOUSAND PESOS (PiP2,3oo,ooo.oo), to be funded by the EccD Council; The term "supplemental Project" refers to site preparation and development, construction of perimeter fence and provision of playground of the NCDC as counterpaft obligation bY the LGU; The parties shall at all times take all necessary action to cooperate with each othei, perform their respective duties and responsibilities using generally accepted professional and technical standards to achieve the objectives of this MOA; The Main project shall be implemented strictly based on the following standard documents to be provided by the ECCD Council: a). Plans/Drawings b). Technical specifications c). Program of Works (POW) and d). Bill of Quantities (BOQ); Funding for the Main Project will be available upon receipt by ECCD Council of the coriesponding Special Allotment Release Order (SARO) and Notice of Cash Allocation (NCA) lrom the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) and shall be released to the LGU upon submission of required documents; procurement activities for the Main Project shall be in accordance with the provisions of Republic Act. WHERE.AS, the contributions of the Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in the country's economic development are highly recognized and deeply appreciated by the government; WHEREAS, the OFWs as steadfast dependable partners in nation-building deserve fast, efficient and effective services from the government; WHEREAS, in cognizance of the need for a more integrated service delivery for easier, more. convenient and less costly access of the public, specifically OFWs to government services, President Rodrigo Roa Duterte ordered all concerned frontline offices to establish a one-stop shop; NOW, THEREFORE, in pursuance of the said directive of the President and as a way of expressing gratitude to all the sacrifices and contributions of OFWs, the parties have agreed, as they hereby agree, to execute this [\Iemorandum of Undertaking and jointly fulfill the obligations herein provided: One-Stop Service Center for OFWs (OSSCO) - There is hereby created a One-Stop Service Center for OFWs in Region Xt, where relevant government agencies engaged in the promotion of the interests and well-being of the overseas Filipino workers (oFWs) shall be represented to efficiently respond to the needs of OFWs. ossco Xl shall adopt and utilize appropriate mechanisms, facirities, equipment and information technology to enable and allow it to respond to the magnitude of OFW's concerns and demands. ossco xl shall be established and operationalized within the premises of Gaisano Mall of Davao Bajada, Davao City, particularly \ t Y \ s at the 5th level, under the overall of xt. Manning of ossco xl- All participating agencies shall assign their respective personnel to deliver the required services stipulated in Annex A of this Undertaking. Functions and Responsibilities - All participating agencies shail have the following general functions and responsibilities: 3.1 Making available to OFWs the needed information as to agency's programs and services, and adequately respond to their queries; 3.2 Providing rationalized and streamlined systems and procedures governing the application for and acquisition of documents required by OFWs in relation to their deployment overseas; 3.3 lmplementing pertinent government rules and regulations relative to the respective mandates of participating agencies; 3.4 3.5 Extending relevant online services adopted by the agency to facilitate processing the documents for deployment overseas; and 4. Eliminating unnecessary and duplicative requirements for deployment overseas Reportorial Requirement - Each participating agency's assigned personnel shall submit a monthly accomplishment report to the mother agency, copy furnished the POEA Xl and the DOLE Xl. As such, operational guidelines shall emanate from DOLE Xl and POEA Xl, subject to the concurrence of the participating agencies. Any and all administrative concerns of the participating agencies and GMall Management shall be coordinated with DOLE Xl and POEA Xl. 5.2 OSSCO Xl's Office Hours: The OSSCO Xl office shall be open from Monday to Friday, from 10:00 A.M. in the morning up to 7:00 P.M. in the evening. Provided further, the participating agencies shall give a written notice to POEA Xl copy furnished the DOLE Xl of any changes to their operating days/hours at least one (1) week prior to the effective date of implementation, for proper dissemination to all concerned. 5.3 Customer Service AssistanUSanitation requirement: To assist OSSCO X! clients, and maintain the clean ess of the common r) .l\a\ ,I \ Eg areas i.e receiving area, customer conference room, one (1) CSA/Sanitation personnel shall be provided by the LGU-Davao City to be assigned at the OSSCO Xl Office, from 10:00 A.M. in the morning up to 7:00 P.M. in the evening, from tVlonday up to Friday, or extend the service during Sundays or holidays when necessary, subject to the approval of the Head of LGU-Davao City or his/her duly authorized representative. text: DEFINffiON OF TERMS - As used in this Ordinance, the following terms shall mean: 1. Children-at-risk (CAR) - refer to children who are vulnerable to and at risk of behaving in a way that can harm themselves or others, or vulnerable and at risk of living, pushed, and exploited to come into conflict with the law because of personal, family, and social circumstances, such as, but not limited to, the following: a. Being abused by any person through sexual, physical, psychological, mental, economic or any other means and the parents or guardians refuse, unwilling or unable to provide protection for the child; b. Being exploited sexually or economically; c. Being abandoned or neglected after diligent search and inquiry where the parents or guardian cannot be found; d. Coming from a dysfunctional or broken family or being without a parent or guardian; e. Being an out of school youth; f . Being street children; g. Being a member of a gang; h. Living in a community with a high level of criminality or drug abuse; i. Living in a situation where armed-conflict is prevalent; j. Committing victimless crimes. 2. Child - referc to a person under eighteen (18) years old and those above 18 but unable to protect themselves and/or physically or mentally incapable of doing so; 3. Interuention - refers to a SERIES of activities which are designed to address issues that cause a child to come into conflict with the law or tend to make the vulnerability in committing offienses. It may take the form of an individualized treatnent program which may include counseling, skills training, education and other activities that will enhance the psychological, emotional and psycho-social well-being of a child; 4. Parent Education - the various forms and alternative means of providing parents with information, skills and suppoft systems to assist them in their needs as their children's primary caregivers and educators. These include public and private parent education programs linked to center homes and media-based children education programs; 5. Transformative Approach are programs and interuentions that create oppoftunities fur CAR to transform as an individual, create enabling community conducive for children, develop community paftnership and volunteerism, enhance responsible parenting and embrace community oriented programs; Ord. No. 0729-t9 6. Children at Risk Transformative Community-Based Center (CARTC) - is the anchor of all community-based and psychosocial care and support program for CAR which will operate 2al7; it will serve as their transformative and transitional home.

It was only in 1848 when the Spanish conquest started to gain a ground following the arrival of Don Jose Cruz de Oyanguren, a native of Vergara, Guipuzcoa in Spain, along with his 70 comrades. The Oyanguren-led group partnered with Datu Daupan, chief of Samal Mandayas, who wanted to get even with Datu Bago. Amid Datu Bago's strong resistance, the foreign group launched massive attacks. Oyanguren ordered the establishment of palisade in Piapi for his defense and installation of causeway across swamps to bring canons within range of Datu Bago's settlement. Navy Commanding General Don Manuel Quesada also joined in the fight against Datu Bago. Their attacks prospered as Datu Bago and his defenders were outgunned, which eventually resulted to Oyanguren's possession of Davao Gulf in 1849. Oyanguren managed to possess the territory despite the lack of support from the government in Manila and his principals. Small progress was made to spur the economy of the gulf region. Oyanguren also urged the different tribes like Mandayas and Manobos to live in settlements to reach them for trade and commerce. The Moros, however, threatened those who would collaborate with the Spaniards. As way to indicate Spanish rule, Oyanguren named the Gulf Region "Nueva Vergara." lt was eventually renamed to "Davao" following the strong clamor of Davaoefios. Davao was derived from three subgroups of Bagobo indigenous peoples as the Tagabawa called the settlement "Dabo," the Guiangan dubbed it "Dawaw" and the Obo tagged it "Davah." The pioneer Christian inhabitants of the area were the proponents behind the official adoption of Davao in 1868. The native inhabitants also became Christians when Jesuit missionaries achieved to pursue conversion of religious faith in 1868. The Jesuit fathers were able to encourage the tribes to live in settlements where they can learn Christian precepts and practices. 1 Excerpts from a manuscript "Davao: An lntroduction to its History" by Ernesto l. Corcino. 2 Moros here is used interchangeably with Muslims, which refers to believers of lslam. Muslim is the preferred usage in lslamic countries in the Middle East, where lslam believers were called Moors before. Moros refer specifically to believers of lslam in Southeastern Philippines as distinguished from the Moors of earlier century, who were lslam believers in Southern Spain and North Africa. 1. The early inhabitants played a vital role to keep Davao Gulf free from foreign dominion. With the stalwart leadership of Davao Gulf Chief Datu Bago, the territory remained unscathed. Some Muslims were urged to become Christians upon the mandate of their leaders, Datu Timan and Datu Porkan, while there were still Muslims who remained steadfast in their lslam faith. Father Saturnino Urios, who labored among the Moros of Hijo in 7892, further swayed the latter's faith that led to the great divide. Those who wanted to live among the Christians left Hijo. They were resettled in Tigatto and Ma-a, under the supervision of Don Francisco Bangoy and Don Teodoro Palma Gil Sr., respectively. The separatist groups refer themselves now as Kagans. The Spaniards' reign in Davao was cut short after 50 years of occupation with the continuous resistance of the Lumads and Moros. They decided to fully abandon Davao in 1899. ln December 1898, the Americans started to colonize Davao. The American settlers, mostly retired soldiers and investors from Zamboanga, Cebu, Manila and United States, recognized the rich potential of Davao for agricultural venture as there were vast areas of primeval forest lands. Noting its rich soil, the Americans started to propagate rubber, abaca and coconut in addition to different varieties of tropical plants imported from Ceylon, lndia, Hawaii, Java and Malaysia. The robust foreign agriculture investments pulled Davao up to serves as one of the major producers of export products such as abaca, copra and lumber in the first two decades of 20th century. Davao also became a regular port of call by inter-island shipping and began direct trade linkages abroad to markets like United states, japan and Australia. ln 1903, Japanese began to arrive as they experienced spike in taxes after Meiji restoration in their country. From recording 30 Japanese in 1903, their population in Davao grew to 20,000 in 1941. One of them was Ohta Kyozaburo who brought 180 Japanese workers from Benguet in 1905. He was among the notable business persons with investments including abaca plantation and general merchandise store. Another investor, Yoshizo Furukawa arrived and began to infuse with a starting capital of P100,000 that grew to F10 million in 1941. The Japanese eventually managed to surpass the Americans in dominating Davao with regards on investments in 1920. The national government also urged the landless persons from Luzon and Visayas to reside in Mindanao. With the growing population, vital infrastructure projects such as roads leading to inaccessible plains were constructed. This move further bolstered the development of Davao. The continuous influx of non-locals and investors buoyed with the economic boom made the municipality to become a City. On October 'J,6, 7936, under the administration of president Manuel L. Quezon in the Commonwealth era, Davao became the chartered City. This was made by virtue of Commonwealth Act No. 51, also known as the Charter of the City of Davao, under the sponsorship of Assemblyman Romualdo C. Quimpo. Davao, as a City, was inaugurated on March 1', L937 with lnterior Secretary Elpidio Quirino, who served as President Quezon's representative in the ceremony. The City's territory spanned 244,OOO hectares that covered the Municipality of Davao and Municipal District of Guianga. ln 7937, the City's population reached 68,000, which further grew to 98,OOO in L940. Despite the toll and dispersion caused by Japanese invasion in December 194L, the City's population increased to 111,253 in 1946. The figures doubled to227,635 in 1950. tt almost hit a millionmark when the City's population reached to 750,000 in L97O, according to population estimates by officials and business sector. But during World War ll, Davao suffered the impact of destruction, causing major setbacks to the City's economic and physical strides. The strong presence of Japanese forces made the City become the subject of American army led by General Mac Arthur to constant bombings, long before the American Liberation Forces landed in Leyte in October 1945. The Japanese forces also established pillboxes and tunnels. The City became the venue where the longest battle campaign took place in the liberation of the Philippines. lt was in mid-August 1945 when the Japanese officials surrendered. Most of the Japanese inhabitants also returned to Japan, leaving their houses and investments in Davao. Thousands of local rebels, meanwhile, managed to infiltrate the Japanese-owned plantations. There was also a deluge of refugees from the mountains, which added to the physical and economic problems of Davao. After the World War ll, rehabilitation efforts were pursued with the assistance from the officials of US Army's PCAU-29. President Manuel Roxas also vowed to distribute properties to the war veterans. Gradually, the City regained its status as the premier agricultural and trade center in Mindanao. Abaca was replaced by other products such as logs, lumber, plywood, copra and banana as the major export commodities. Fruits like mangoes and bananas were produced for country-wide consumption. Thousands of manual miners also started to extract precious metals in Mt. Diwata, Northern Davao and eastern side of Davao Gulf in Boringot, Pantukan. ln 1955, Davao City was finally granted to conduct elections for local government positions, including mayor, vice mayor and 10 councilors, following the enactment of the national law. Mayor Carmelo Porras emerged as the first chief executive of the City, who was elected in November 1955. Davao City was also made independent after the division of Davao province into different provinces such as Davao del Norte, Davao del Sur and Davao Oriental. lt is now also known as a highly urbanized City with over 1.6 million populace and P7.3 billion income as of 2016. Today, Davao City has become a bustling metropolis. The City's economy spurred along with local and foreign investments that continue to buoy up. This is a testament that Davao City's immense growth will incessantly rise, moving upward beyond the towering edifice. ETHNICITY AND IANGUAGE The City brewed with diversity. There was a mixture of Lumads, Moros and ethnic groups from other parts of the country. The migration of inhabitants from Luzon and Visayas and some parts of Mindanao make the urban center the "Melting Pot of the Philippines." Amid the presence of diversity, majority of the populace prefer to speak Cebuano, Tagalog and English as way to understand with each other. The local dialects of Lumads and Moros, meanwhile, remain alive especially in their respective communities mostly at the Second and Third Districts. Among the tribes, Sama, Ata, Kagan, Maguindanao, K'lata, Obu-Manuvu, lranon, Tausug, Tagabawa, Matigsalog and Maranao are based in Davao City. The tribes sprawled across the City, including the Bagobos who resided from upper Bangkal to Catalunan, Ula and Biao. Of the indigenous peoples' tribes, the Atas were the earliest natives who inhabited in Davao. Most of the Bagobos, on the other hand, intermarried with the Spaniards, Americans and Japanese. VISION AND MISSION STATEMENT VISION STATEMENT We envision Davao City as a globally livable City and a center of excellence in governance, investment, tourism, climate change adaptation, disaster resiliency, and sustainable growth driven by empowered citizenry. MrssroN Ensure effective and efficient delivery of services through responsive leadership and com petent huma n resources. Sustain the gains by ensuring that the people of Davao are empowered, protected and secure, and gender and culturally sensitive to attain the best quality of life. Continue to engage participative citizenry in resource-based, market-driven economic activities within the context of balanced ecology, and equity-led development. Develop a progressive and future-proof network of infrastructure, utilities, and support services. Maintain a disaster-resilient, climate change-adaptive, and ecologically balanced environment through ridge-to-reef approach, proper solid waste management, preservation of natural environment, promotion of renewable energy, and adoption of low carbon and eco-friendly technologies. CORE VALUES o Leadership o Good Governance and Service Excellence o Resiliency and Unity o lntegrity a a a a a Sectoral Mission Statement Economic To become a major growth pole in the international market by engaging its empowered citizenry in resource based and market-driven economic activities within the context of balanced ecology, sustainable growth and equity-led development. Davao City aims to be the growth center in Mindanao. To attain this, it is going to engage the "players" in the local economy to engage in propulsive industries, industries with export potentials and light, medium and heavy industries such as in agri-based industries. Moreover, Davao City shall be developed as the service, financial, tourism destination, and education center in Mindanao. Social Make Davao City and its people, free from cold, hunger and disease, unburdened by ignorance, secure in their persons and domicile, enjoying the blessing of growth and development without sacrificing the quality of the environment. Strive to empower the Davao City residents by allowing their genuine participation in the formulation of decision affecting them. Recognize the right of the Muslim People and Tribal Filipinos to self-determination and to give due respect to their ancestral domain and their culture. The City will adopt a policy in ensuring their welfare and well-being. Ensure the full implementation of programs geared to uphold the survival, protection, development and participation for the rights of children especially those in extremely difficult circumstances. Engender policy, strategies, programs and projects to be more responsive to specific gender needs. ln essence, all programs shall be deeply rooted to the conviction that all development changes are people-centered. lnfrastructure and Utilities To provide Davao City with adequate, relevant and efficient infrastructure support facilities, utilities, and urban basic services in order to attain the socio-economic upliftment of its citizenry within the framework of sustainable development. The delivery of urban basic services is primarily the responsibility of the city government. Basic services include the provision of water, electricity, public transportation and sanitation facilities (drainage, sewerage, toilet, garbage collection and disposal). Local Government Administration We commit to transform Davao City's vision into reality by providing excellent and effective services, anchored on the principle of "leadership by example" and establish mechanisms that will ensure efficient and effective governance. Land Use Sector Our mission is to transform Davao City into a modern and a well planned investment center in Mindanao and the Asia-Pacific region, propelled by socially enlightened leaders and empowered citizenry, spiritually committed to attain sustainable growth and optimum development within the context of balance ecology.
